stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In a six-year study of three neighboring wolf packs in northern Minnesota, ecologist Ana Ruiz found that territorial boundaries shifted far more than expected. Each pack defended a small core area all year, but during deep-snow winters the ______ expanded as moose moved down into the river valleys, and the overlap between them nearly doubled.
explanation: Check each noun. "Ranges" owns nothing. It comes right before the verb "expanded," so it is a plain plural with no apostrophe. "Packs" owns the ranges, so it needs an apostrophe. Now count the owners. The study follows three packs, and "the overlap between them" means the ranges of several packs are being compared. So there is more than one owner, and a plural owner ending in s takes s'. "Packs' ranges" is the only choice with that combination.

A.why: You saw that the packs own the ranges, but the singular "Each pack" just before the blank pulled you toward one owner. The passage tracks three packs whose ranges overlap, and no single pack is ever named as "the pack," so the owner has to be plural: packs'.

B.why: You got "ranges" right as a plain plural, but you left out the apostrophe on "packs." The packs own the ranges, so "packs" has to show possession.

D.why: You got the owner right, but you also added an apostrophe to "ranges." Ranges don't own anything. They are the subject of "expanded," and the noun right before a verb never takes an apostrophe.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Nutrition scientists have long asked whether eating late at night raises blood sugar no matter what is eaten. In a 2024 trial run jointly by two university labs, 48 adults ate identical dinners at either 6 p.m. or 10 p.m. Because the ______ were matched in calories and composition, the researchers attributed the higher glucose readings after late dinners to timing alone.
explanation: There are three nouns here, so check each one. "Meals" comes right before the verb "were" and owns nothing, so it takes no apostrophe. "Participants" owns the meals, and there are 48 adults, so that's a plural owner: participants'. "Trial" owns the participants. The passage describes one trial ("a 2024 trial") even though two labs ran it, so that's a single owner: trial's. Only "trial's participants' meals" has all three pieces right.

A.why: You read "two university labs" and counted two trials. The labs ran a single trial together ("a 2024 trial run jointly"), so the owner is one trial: trial's. You got the other two nouns right, but the plural owner on the first noun makes this choice wrong.

C.why: You saw that the participants own the meals, but you wrote them as a single owner. The trial had 48 adults, so the owner is plural: participants'.

D.why: You got both owners right, but you added an apostrophe to "meals." Meals don't own anything. They are the subject of "were," and the last noun before a verb never takes an apostrophe.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: To test whether colony size affects nest-building speed, ornithologist Ana Ruiz monitored cliff swallows at two colonies on the same river bluff. Each colony drew its mud from a single shared bank, so differences between the two ______ could not be blamed on building material. Swallows in the larger colony nonetheless finished their nests in about half the time.
explanation: The colonies own the nests, so the first noun needs an apostrophe. "The two" tells you there is more than one owner, so the plural possessive colonies' is right. The nests don't own anything, since they come right before the verb "could," so they take no apostrophe.

A.why: You let "Each colony" in the previous clause decide the owner count. But "between the two" names two owners, so the singular colony's contradicts the passage.

C.why: You moved the apostrophe to the wrong noun. The colonies are the owners. The nests come right before a verb and own nothing, so nests' puts punctuation where it does no grammatical work.

D.why: You got the owner right but then gave the nests an apostrophe too. Nests' own nothing here, so nest's is both possessive and singular when the word should be a plain plural.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Under Fairport's 2019 growth plan, each of the city's four districts drafted its own zoning code. Hillcrest, the smallest, moved fastest: by the following spring, nearly all of the ______ had been rezoned to allow shops on the ground floor and apartments above, while the other three districts were still holding public hearings.
explanation: The owner here is Hillcrest alone, the district that "moved fastest." One owner takes 's, so you want district's. The parcels come right before "had been rezoned" and own nothing, so they stay a plain plural.

A.why: You took "four districts" from the first sentence as the owner count. But the colon narrows the sentence to Hillcrest alone, and the other three are still in hearings, so a plural owner contradicts the passage.

B.why: The owner is right, but you also gave parcels an apostrophe. Parcels are the subject of "had been rezoned" and own nothing, so they take no apostrophe.

D.why: You switched the roles. The district is the owner and needs an apostrophe. Parcels own nothing, so parcels' puts the apostrophe on the wrong word.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: At the Taller Verde print studio, each woodcut edition is pulled by a team of several printers rather than by a single artist. To credit that shared labor, the ______ are written in pencil beneath every impression, alongside the edition number.
explanation: This blank has two owners in a chain. The studio owns the printers, and there is one studio, so you need studio's. The printers own the initials, and there are "several printers," so you need printers'. The initials come right before "are written" and stay plain.

A.why: You got the studio right, then let "each woodcut edition" or "a single artist" make the printer singular. The passage says several printers share the work, so printer's contradicts it.

B.why: The printers are right, but studios has no apostrophe even though it owns the printers. It is also plural when the passage names one studio.

C.why: You reversed both owner counts. The passage names one studio and several printers, but this choice makes the studios plural and the printer singular.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Every map in the 1842 Hallam atlas was drawn by a different surveyor, and it shows. Historians comparing the ______ have found that no two maps use the same symbol for a mountain pass; one marks passes with a small arch, another with a pair of crossed lines.
explanation: The historians compare legends across maps ("no two maps"), so there are several owners and you need the plural possessive maps'. The legends are the object of "comparing" and own nothing, so they stay a plain plural.

B.why: You let "Every map" make the owner singular. But a finding that "no two maps" agree needs legends from many maps, so one map's legends contradicts the passage.

C.why: You put the apostrophe on the legends instead of the maps. The maps are the owners, and the legends own nothing.

D.why: This makes the owner singular and also gives legend an apostrophe it doesn't need. The legends own nothing.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When a single employer dominates a local job market, economists call the result monopsony. In Lena Ortiz's study of Carver Falls, a mill town where one firm employed nearly four hundred residents, the ______ rose more slowly over the decade than those in comparable towns with several competing employers.
explanation: The study covers one town, Carver Falls, so you need town's. That town's workers own the wages, and there are "nearly four hundred" of them, so you need workers'. The wages come right before "rose" and stay plain.

A.why: You let "comparable towns" make the owner plural. The study is about one town. You also left the workers without an apostrophe and gave one to wages, which owns nothing.

B.why: You got the town right but made the worker singular. The passage counts nearly four hundred workers, so worker's contradicts it.

D.why: The workers are right, but towns has no apostrophe even though it owns the workers, and it is plural when the study covers one town.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: The common octopus has roughly 500 million neurons, a number comparable to that of a dog. Strikingly, about two-thirds of an ______ are located not in its central brain but in its eight arms, which can taste and grip without direct instructions from the head.
explanation: The article "an" and the later "its" both point to one octopus, so the owner takes 's: octopus's. The neurons come right before "are located" and own nothing, so they stay a plain plural.

A.why: You heard the general claim about the species and made the owner plural. But "an" can only come before a singular noun, and "its" refers back to one animal.

C.why: The owner is right, but neurons are the subject of "are located" and own nothing, so they take no apostrophe.

D.why: This leaves the owner without an apostrophe and gives one to neurons instead, so both nouns are wrong.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Afrikaans developed from the Dutch spoken by seventeenth-century settlers at the Cape, and the two languages still share most of their vocabulary. As a result, the two ______ can often read each other's newspapers with ease, even when following rapid conversation proves much harder.
explanation: The speakers belong to both languages, and "the two" names two owners, so you need languages'. The speakers come right before "can" and own nothing, so they stay a plain plural.

B.why: You made the owner singular. "The two" in this sentence, like the two languages in the one before, means there are two owners.

C.why: You put the apostrophe on speakers, which comes right before the verb and owns nothing. The languages are the owners.

D.why: This makes the owner singular and adds an apostrophe to speaker, which owns nothing. That gives you the wrong count and the wrong form.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Three automated weather stations ring the Tassel Valley, but when last October's windstorm struck, only the one on Calder Ridge kept recording through the peak gusts. That ______ were later used to recalibrate wind forecasts for the entire valley, including the two sites whose sensors had failed.
explanation: "That" points back to the single station on Calder Ridge, so there is one owner and it takes 's. The readings come right before "were" and own nothing, so they stay a plain plural.

A.why: You let "Three automated weather stations" decide the owner count. But "That" can only refer to one station, and the passage says only one kept recording.

B.why: The owner is right, but you also gave the readings an apostrophe. They are the subject of "were" and own nothing.

C.why: This puts the apostrophe on the readings instead of the station and makes the owner plural, so both nouns are wrong.
